newsitem.title: UK: Dlr breaks above 1.70 marks at European close.
newsitem.headline: Dlr breaks above 1.70 marks at European close.

text.p: The dollar zoomed above 1.70 marks for the first time since April 1994 at the European close, continuing its relentless rise on the back of solid economic fundamentals, dealers said.

The dollar was bid up to a fresh 34-month high against the German unit mark but failed to make much headway above 1.70 marks due to lack of follow-through buying as U.S. markets were closed for a holiday. But 1.70 marks is not the limit yet, analysts said.
"The outlook for the dollar is still positive, in view of continued economic problems in Germany and Japan," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
At 1615 GMT the dollar traded at 1.6999/7009 marks, just off the 1.7003 high and up from 1.6876/79 at the European close on Friday. Against the yen, it was at 124.35/45, up from 124.20/25.
Dollar/Swiss was at 1.4814/24 francs, from a high of 1.4820 and compared with 1.4635/45 late on Friday.
Against the yen, the dollar was also invigorated but concern that central banks might intervene to stem its rise capped a lid on dollar/yen.
Intervention fears were stoked overnight by a news agency report that Japan and the U.S. had agreed Japan would buy dollars independently if the yen dropped sharply.
Japan is generally believed to be the least happy of the G3 with persistent dollar strength, meaning the market has focused on the Bank of Japan for possible central bank action.
But the Bundesbank last week joined the protest against further dollar gains, and its vice-president Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum told Reuters today he saw no reason for a weaker mark.
But with players convinced that fundamentals favour a strong dollar, unilateral -- or even concerted -- intervention is unlikely to cool their ardour, traders and analysts said.
The rally has been fired by relatively higher U.S. rates, the prospect of solid growth and dollar-positive capital flows.

"If the market feels it's only odd people within G7 who want this to stop, or they feel they're only going to have a tickle with it, I think the market will take the dollar higher," said Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at Bank of Boston here.
"It requires a fundamental reassessment of econonomic prospects for the dollar's recent trend to finish," said Lyons.
This would require a significant deterioration in expectations about U.S. growth or a more upbeat assessment of economic prospects in Germany or Japan.
Lyons said the only data on the horizon, which could cause the markets to rethink, would be a sharp rise in the German Ifo business sentiment survey for January, due later this week.
But DKB expects the index to rise just slightly, from 95.8 to 96.9 as Germany's economy remains plagued by high unemployment and weak economic growth.

The mark was steady on its European crosses. It showed little reaction to comments by Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who said he will not ask for an easing of the criteria for membership of the single European currency and that there was no reason to delay Italy's participation in EMU.
Mark/lira was at 987.30/60 against 984.40/90 late on Friday.
